newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand hopes to stay on top of rubber market.
newsitem.headline: Thailand hopes to stay on top of rubber market.

text.p: Thailand expects to remain a major world player in natural rubber in the next century but will focus on improving local rubber-based manufacturing rather than depend on exports, a senior official said on Monday.

Sanit Samosorn, deputy director-general of the Agriculture Ministry's agriculture department, said annual production would rise to between 2.2 million and 2.5 million tonnes between the years 2000 and 2010.
Thailand expects to produce 1.88 million tonnes this year.
Sanit was speaking to Reuters after addressing the Asia International Rubber Conference.
"The government has plans to increase the domestic consumption of natural rubber to 25 percent of total production by the year 2000 from less than 10 percent now," he said.

"The Board of Investment is offering incentives on rubber-based manufacturing...such as auto-related rubber products or gloves, while acceleration of training and transfers of technologies are in place," he said.
Growth in Thailand's vehicle industry would spur domestic demand for rubber as the industry was expected to remain the biggest outlet for rubber consumption in Thailand.
Sanit said total sales of motor vehicles in 1996 are expected to reach 650,000 units, up 13.7 percent from 1995.

On the supply side, the government also planned to maintain Thailand's competitive edge as the world's biggest producer by shifting the rubber production base from the southern peninsula to the northeastern region, Sanit said.
The shift would help alleviate problems, such as shortages of land and labour in the south, which have threatened the industry, he said in his speech.

"At present, the northeast has great potential for rubber production with at least 1.6 million hectares (four million acres) which is suitable for rubber cultivation ... Not only is the land cheaper, more labour is also available," he said.
The total rubber area in Thailand is presently about 1.80 million hectares (4.5 million acres), of which 1.55 million hectares (3.87 million acres) are in the south.
A favourable climate in the south makes the area more suitable for high-value crops other than rubber, such as exotic fruits, fast growing timber and oil palm, Sanit said.
Thailand has been the world's largest producer and exporter of natural rubber since 1991.
Exports this year are forecast to reach 1.69 million tonnes and will rise to around 1.99 million tonnes in the year 2000, for total export value of at least 35 billion baht ($1.4 billion).
